_about: Pre/post concept test for Module 5 (network pharmacology). 'answer' is the index of the correct option. Check the science before using with students.

questions.q: What does a drug-target network show that docking one protein does not?
options: The exact binding energy
All the proteins a drug may affect, and how they connect with the disease
The crystal structure of the target
The half-life of the drug
questions.why: Docking looks at one protein at a time. A network widens the view to many proteins and pathways.

options: A drug acting on several targets
Taking several drugs together
A drug made of several chemicals
A drug with several doses
questions.why: The word describes one molecule affecting many proteins.

questions.q: In the workflow, the 'candidate targets' are:
options: The genes with the highest degree
The genes found in both the drug-target list and the disease-gene list
All genes in the disease list
Genes with a binding energy below -7
questions.why: The overlap is the first filter. Hubs and pathways come later.

questions.q: A prediction tool gives a target a probability of 0.000. How should it be treated?
options: As a certain target
As noise, not a real prediction
As the strongest target
As proof the drug is inactive
questions.why: A score of zero means the tool found no support. It is not evidence for or against binding.

questions.q: Using a very strict score cut-off for targets can:
options: Make the network more complete
Remove real targets that happen to have low scores
Always improve accuracy
Add more false links
questions.why: Thresholds trade false positives for false negatives. Unusual compounds often score low even when they bind.

questions.q: What does the interaction confidence cut-off (for example 0.7) decide?
options: How many proteins the drug binds
Which interactions you believe enough to draw
The binding energy
The size of the proteins
questions.why: A low cut-off gives a dense, speculative network. A high cut-off gives a sparse one.

questions.q: A protein has a very high betweenness. What does it mean?
options: It has the most links
It lies on many shortest paths between other proteins, like a bridge
It binds the drug most tightly
It is the least studied protein
questions.why: Betweenness measures bridging. Degree counts links. They need not agree.

questions.q: Why can well-studied proteins look like hubs?
options: They really have more interactions in the cell
More experiments exist for them, so more interactions have been recorded
They are bigger proteins
They are always drug targets
questions.why: Study bias is a known problem of interaction databases. A hub may simply be a popular protein.

questions.q: Why are p-values corrected (for example Benjamini-Hochberg) in pathway enrichment?
options: The test is always wrong
Many pathways are tested at once, so some will look significant by chance
To make results look better
Because the sample is too large
questions.why: The more tests you run, the more false positives appear. The correction controls this.

questions.q: A network analysis ends with a significant pathway. What is the best conclusion?
options: The mechanism is proven
A hypothesis to test in experiments
The drug is safe
No more work is needed
questions.why: Network pharmacology generates hypotheses. Confirmation needs laboratory data.
